title: AI video disclosure guide: when and how to label synthetic media
summary: When to label AI-generated video on YouTube, TikTok and Instagram, with exact disclosure examples, a six-step workflow and a pre-publication checklist.
body_markdown:
## Quick answer


**Label realistic AI-generated or meaningfully altered video when it could be mistaken for a real person, place, event, speech or recording.**


YouTube, TikTok and Meta have different controls; use the destination’s current native disclosure setting, then explain the change in ordinary language when context matters. A label does not replace consent, rights clearance or a sponsorship disclosure.


This guide answers a narrow production question: what should a viewer know about a synthetic video before believing or sharing it? It is separate from[commercial-use and rights clearance](https://magichour.ai/blog/can-you-use-ai-generated-videos-commercially) . Platform rules change, so check the linked policy at upload time. The examples below are editorial scenarios, not claims about a tested Magic Hour output.


## The decision in 30 seconds


Ask two questions: **Is the result realistic?** Could it make a viewer believe a real person said or did something, a real place or event was shown, or a recording is authentic when it is not? If yes, use the destination’s AI disclosure control. Then ask what a viewer still could misunderstand. A short caption such as “AI-generated scene; no real event is depicted” often explains more than a bare #AI tag.


Keep three separate records: AI alteration, permission to use source material or likeness, and any paid or material connection to a brand. Passing one check does not pass the others. This is a practical editorial framework, not legal advice.


## What the major platforms currently ask for


**YouTube.**[YouTube’s GenAI disclosure guidance](https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/14328491) calls for disclosure when AI meaningfully alters or generates photorealistic content: for example, making a real person seem to say something they did not say, altering footage of a real event or place, or depicting a realistic scene that never occurred. It says minor aesthetic edits and clearly non-realistic content generally do not need this disclosure. In YouTube Studio, answer the “AI use” question in the upload attributes. Check the published watch page afterward; label placement can vary.


**TikTok.**[TikTok’s AI-generated content policy](https://support.tiktok.com/en/using-tiktok/creating-videos/ai-generated-content) requires creators to label AI-generated content containing realistic images, audio or video, and encourages labels for content significantly edited by AI. Its examples include changed speech, a transformed real event and a face swap that substantially changes a subject. For a video post, TikTok describes the AI-generated content setting under More options before posting. If a TikTok AI effect supplies the only alteration, TikTok may label it automatically; an additional independent AI edit still needs its own assessment.


**Facebook and Instagram.**[Meta’s explanation of AI-content labels](https://about.fb.com/news/2024/04/metas-approach-to-labeling-ai-generated-content-and-manipulated-media/) describes “AI info” labels that can follow detected signals or creator disclosure. Meta has said users should disclose photorealistic AI video or realistic-sounding altered audio. The controls and display may differ by app and post type, so check the current upload flow and the published post rather than assuming an exported file’s metadata will produce the right label.


These are platform policies, not a universal legal rule. A creator posting the same clip to three destinations should evaluate and label it in each upload flow.


## A six-step disclosure workflow


**1. Describe what changed.** Write one sentence before exporting: “The footage is real but the speaker’s voice was synthetically changed,” or “The entire scene was generated; it did not happen.” Name the meaningful alteration, not just the software used.


**2. Classify realism and risk.** Review the final clip with the sound on and off. Could a reasonable viewer mistake the person, place, event, speech, endorsement or product demonstration for a real recording? High-stakes contexts such as news, health, finance and elections warrant especially explicit context. A cartoon dragon is different from a realistic fabricated arrest.


**3. Clear inputs and claims.** Record who owns the footage, music, image, voice and likeness, and whether the people depicted agreed to this use. Verify statements and product claims separately. A conspicuous AI label cannot authorize an unlicensed asset or a fake testimonial.


**4. Select the platform control.** On YouTube, answer the AI-use upload question. On TikTok, check the AI-generated content setting under More options for a video. On Meta apps, review the current AI disclosure option presented for that post. Do this for each destination; do not assume cross-posting carries a label over.


**5. Add human-readable context.** Say what changed in the caption or in-video text where confusion is likely. “AI-generated visualization of a proposed store; not footage of a built location” is clearer than “Made with AI.” If the content is a paid endorsement, address that relationship independently and prominently.


**6. Verify the published result.** Inspect the live post on a phone and another logged-out view if available. Confirm the platform label, caption and any in-video disclosure survive cropping, description truncation and reposting. Save the source, approved script, export, policy link and screenshot of the final post for later correction.


### Create a clearly labeled example


Make one original short clip, record what was generated, and decide how you will describe it before uploading. Review the final platform label and caption on a second device.

## Three examples of useful disclosure copy


**Fictional scene.** A realistic AI-generated street scene could be mistaken for footage of a real incident. Use the platform AI setting and add: “AI-generated fictional scene; no real incident is shown.” For a clearly fantastical animation, first check the destination’s threshold; do not mechanically label every minor AI-assisted edit.


**Altered executive video.** If a real executive approved a translated AI dub and lip-sync, use: “The speaker approved this translation; voice and lip movements were altered with AI.” Record approval and script review. If the person did not approve it, a label is not a substitute for consent and the video should not be published.


**Product visualization.** If an AI animation shows how an unbuilt product might operate, use: “AI-generated visualization of a proposed feature; not recorded product footage.” Review every visible specification and avoid implying that the product exists or performs as animated. An ad may also need a separate brand-relationship disclosure.


## If the disclosure disappears after posting


Treat a missing or incorrect label as a publication defect. First save the URL and a screenshot showing the viewer experience. Reopen the upload or edit controls to see whether the AI setting was saved. If the platform permits correction, update the setting and caption, then verify the public post again. If the control cannot be fixed or a misleading version has already circulated, pause promotion and consider removing and reposting the corrected export. Record which version was live and when. Do not quietly swap the creative while leaving viewers with an old, false claim.


A reposted clip may lose the original platform label, and an edited vertical cut may hide an in-video note at the edge of the frame. Recheck every crop and destination separately. Keep plain-language text inside the safe area when the context is important even without the surrounding caption, such as a clipped repost or a video embedded on another site.


## Make the wording specific to the alteration


“Made with AI” tells viewers almost nothing about the edit. Name the changed element: “The background is AI-generated; the interview audio is unaltered,” “The voice is an approved translation of the original speech,” or “This product shot is an AI visualization; the shown feature is not available.” Use the shortest truthful wording that prevents the likely misunderstanding. Avoid calling a fully generated scene “enhanced footage,” and do not imply a real person approved words that were written by someone else.


For documentary, customer evidence, testimonials and product demonstrations, put the disclosure where it will be seen before the viewer relies on the claim. A platform label is useful, but the context may call for visible text in the video itself. If a brand relationship also exists, state that separately. Review the opening seconds, muted playback, captions and small-screen crop. These checks are editorial recommendations, not a claim that each platform mandates the same presentation.


## When an AI label is not enough


Disclosure does not cure impersonation, deceptive endorsements or missing rights. TikTok says some AI depictions remain prohibited even when labeled. In the United States, the[FTC’s influencer disclosure guidance](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/disclosures-101-social-media-influencers) says a material brand relationship should be clearly disclosed; for a video endorsement, that disclosure should be in the video, not only its description. An AI-content label and a sponsorship disclosure answer different questions.


Do not rely on an invisible metadata flag, a hashtag below “more,” or an upload-setting screenshot as your only proof. Policies and interfaces change. If a platform automatically applies a label, inspect what viewers actually see and correct factual context in the creative or caption where needed.


## Pre-publication checklist


Before posting, confirm: (1) the source and likeness permissions; (2) the factual claims and any endorsement; (3) whether the final video is realistic or materially altered under each destination’s current rule; (4) the native AI setting; (5) plain-language context where a label alone would mislead; (6) any separate sponsorship disclosure; and (7) a screenshot of the published result. If any answer is uncertain, hold the upload and resolve it.
